newsitem.title: UK: West cut funding for energy research 1985-95 - IEA.
newsitem.headline: West cut funding for energy research 1985-95 - IEA.

text.p: Western government spending on energy research declined in the decade to 1995 with coal and nuclear power bearing the brunt of cuts while oil, gas and renewable energy enjoyed funding increases, the West's oil watchdog said.

An International Energy Agency (IEA) report on energy technology research and development said several of the 22 industrialised countries surveyed had cut such funding by over 75 percent between 1985 and 1995.

"Overall government budgets relating to coal and nuclear energy technologies have declined very substantially in some countries, while recent support for renewable energy is increasing," the report said.
"Energy conservation budgets have increased since 1985."
U.S. spending on energy research and development fell to $2.9 billion in 1995 from $3.2 billion in 1985, the IEA said.

Smaller countries showed larger percentage cuts. Portugal's spending on such funding fell to $3.8 million in 1995 from $17.4 million in 1988. That of Sweden fell to $64 million in 1995 from $162 million in 1985.
Total spending on energy research and development in the 22 countries fell to $10 billion in 1995 from $12.5 billion in 1985.
The Paris-based agency said an important trend was a shift in spending priorities increasingly to short-term rather than long-term needs.
Increasing industrial competition and greater liberalisation in utility industries was encouraging shorter timetables in research and development investments.
Spending on oil and gas and on conservation showed the sharpest increases over the decade, with spending on coal showing the steepest fall.

The agency said energy technology was increasingly related to research and development in other scientific fields and its support could be a part of an attempt to meet other goals such as protecting the environment.

The IEA said its figures did not fully reflect support allocated to non-energy technologies -- such as development of high-temperature materials -- that nevertheless produced benefits applicable to the energy industry.
Figures are in million dollars at 1995 prices. Statistics are drawn from country submissions and the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development's Economic Outlook.
